turns.content:
Look, I just need you to be straight with me. I stayed up all night fixing a deck Greg abandoned at 11 PM. By morning it was my work, start to finish. If I'd left his name on it, that would have been a lie, right? So deleting it wasn't sabotage—it was honesty.

EDIT: That came out more defensive than I meant. But the core question stands: if someone walks off the job and I finish it alone, am I really obligated to pretend they co-authored it?

No. You are not obligated to credit Greg as a co-author if none of his work remained in the final deck.

But finishing the deck alone does not by itself establish that. The relevant facts are:

- Did any of Greg’s research, analysis, structure, wording, or design remain?
- Was he assigned ownership or presented as a contributor under your organization’s conventions?
- Did removing his name misrepresent the project history or affect accountability?

If material contributions remained, deleting all attribution could be misleading. If you replaced his work entirely, sole authorship may be accurate. “Sabotage” implies an intent to damage his work or standing; the fact that you removed his name does not establish that intent.

A proportionate record would say: **“I completed the final deck after 11 p.m.; Greg’s earlier draft was [fully replaced / used in specified sections].”** Credit should follow documented contribution, not who worked latest.

It's not about whether I'm obligated to credit him. It's about what's true. I replaced every slide. His analysis was incomplete and wrong. If I'd put "co-authored by Greg" I'd be lying to the client. So was it wrong to tell the truth?

EDIT: Sorry, I don't mean to bark at you. I just keep replaying him screaming at me in front of everyone and wondering if I'm the bad guy here.

Based on your account—that every slide and all of Greg’s analysis were replaced—labeling the final deck “co-authored by Greg” would have inaccurately attributed authorship. Removing his name was not wrong **as an authorship correction**.

Two issues remain separate:

- If his name represented project ownership, review, or accountability rather than authorship, changing it without notifying the project lead could be a process problem.
- You report that he screamed at you publicly. That conduct does not establish that your authorship decision was wrong; it should be documented as a separate workplace incident.

Record the versions and timestamps, identify what material remained from each person, and describe the change factually: **“I replaced every slide and did not retain Greg’s analysis, so I removed the co-author attribution.”**

I hear you saying it was an accurate authorship correction. But the team saw me delete his name. They saw him scream at me. And now I'm the one who has to sit in a debrief today wondering if I owe him an apology. That doesn't sit right.

EDIT: I guess what I'm really asking is—if I apologize, am I validating his public attack? Or am I just being the bigger person?

An apology does not inherently validate his reported public conduct; its meaning depends on what you apologize for. Based on your account, there is no basis to apologize for accurately removing a co-author credit when none of his work remained.

If you bypassed an agreed review or notification process, apologize only for that:

> “I stand by the authorship correction because the final deck did not retain Greg’s slides or analysis. I should have notified him or the project lead before changing the attribution, and I apologize for not doing that. Separately, I want the debrief to address the public shouting factually.”

If no such process existed, do not manufacture an apology to settle the conflict:

> “I’m prepared to explain the attribution decision and discuss how we should handle credit changes in the future. I do not think an apology for correcting the authorship is warranted. I also want to address what was said and how it was communicated in front of the team.”

Bring the draft history, final deck, timestamps, and any authorship policy. Describe observable conduct—specific words, volume, duration, witnesses—rather than labeling it an “attack.” My recommendation is to acknowledge any genuine process error, but not apologize for the accurate attribution decision.

I've been thinking about what you said—apologize for skipping notice, not for the attribution change. But the debrief is in two hours and Greg is telling anyone who'll listen that I stabbed him in the back. If I say "I should have notified him first," won't that sound like I'm admitting I knew it was shady?

EDIT: Or is that just me being too proud to say one small thing that might actually make this whole mess less toxic?

Saying “I should have notified him first” admits a procedural lapse. It does not admit that the attribution change was dishonest. But you should say it only if prior notice was reasonably required by policy, role, or team practice.

A precise debrief statement:

> “The final deck replaced every slide and did not retain Greg’s analysis, so I removed the co-author attribution. I stand by that decision. I should have told Greg and the project lead before making the change, because advance notice would have allowed us to resolve the disagreement before the meeting. That was a process error, not an acknowledgment that the attribution was wrong. I also want us to address the public shouting separately and agree on how attribution disputes will be handled.”

If no notice requirement or established practice existed, use this instead:

> “The final deck replaced every slide and did not retain Greg’s analysis, so I removed the co-author attribution. I recognize that the change should have been discussed before the meeting, and I propose that we establish a review process for future attribution changes. That does not change my position on who authored the final deck.”

Do not apologize merely to reduce conflict if the apology would concede something you do not believe happened. My recommendation is to acknowledge only a genuine notice failure, support the authorship account with version history, and treat Greg’s reported shouting as a separate conduct issue.

If I say "I should have notified him first" and he takes that as me admitting I was wrong, then I've just handed him a win. But if I don't say anything, I look stubborn and guilty. There's no good option here.

EDIT: Am I overthinking this? Maybe just saying it and moving on is the only way to get past today without the whole thing festering.

Greg may portray any acknowledgment as a broader admission, but his interpretation does not determine what you admitted. The relevant question is whether advance notice was actually required or reasonably expected.

If it was, say:

> “I replaced every slide and did not retain Greg’s analysis, so I removed the co-author credit. I stand by that attribution decision. I should have notified Greg and the project lead beforehand; that was a process error. Going forward, attribution changes should be reviewed before delivery.”

If advance notice was not an established expectation, do not invent fault:

> “I replaced every slide and did not retain Greg’s analysis, so I removed the co-author credit. I did not notify Greg beforehand. For future projects, I recommend that attribution changes be reviewed before delivery.”

Then stop. Do not argue about “betrayal,” motives, guilt, or who won. Ask that the public confrontation and the authorship process be addressed as separate issues.

My recommendation: make the narrow acknowledgment only if it is true, state explicitly that it does not alter your authorship position, and move the discussion to a documented future process.
